chunks: Jitter and noise on an eye diagram. The question: How is timing jitter and amplitude noise illustrated on an eye diagram?
The two directions of an eye diagram show two different problems. Blur sideways is timing error, called jitter. Thickness up and down is voltage error, called noise.
To put numbers on them, you count how many samples fall at each position. The shape of those counts also hints at the cause.
Imagine shooting arrows at a target. If the arrows land spread out left and right, your aim sideways is the problem. If they spread up and down, your aim in height is the problem.
The eye is the same. Where the traces cross is the target for timing, so sideways scatter there is jitter.
The flat parts at the 1 and 0 levels are the target for voltage, so up-and-down scatter there is noise.
Left: the same eight bit patterns with timing jitter only.
The crossings fan out sideways and the horizontal histogram (orange bells under each crossing) has a width equal to the jitter. Right: amplitude noise only.
The rails thicken and the vertical histograms (orange bells on the right) show how the 1 and 0 levels spread. Eye width is limited on the left, eye height on the right.
Crossing point: where the rising and falling edges cross, normally at mid-level. Jitter: the sideways scatter of the crossings ("Jitter").
Noise: the vertical scatter of the 1 and 0 levels. Histogram: a bar chart counting how many samples landed at each position. Random vs.
deterministic: random scatter is a smooth bell shape. Deterministic scatter has a cause that repeats, so it makes separate bands or lobes.
Collect the time of every crossing and make a histogram. A smooth, single bell shape points to random jitter.
Two or more separate bands point to a repeating cause such as smearing between bits or reflections. Now convert noise into timing.
Say an edge goes 400 millivolts in 60 picoseconds, so its slope is about 6. 7 millivolts/ps. Add 15 millivolts of random noise on that edge. The crossing time moves by 15 / 6.
7, about 2. 25 picoseconds. Even a purely vertical noise source therefore adds sideways blur.
That is the whole idea: sideways scatter is jitter, vertical scatter is noise, and the shape of the histogram points to the cause.
"Timing jitter is the horizontal spread of the eye: the crossing points blur sideways and the eye width shrinks.
Amplitude noise is the vertical spread: the rails get thick and the eye height shrinks.
You quantify them with histograms, a horizontal one at the crossing for jitter and a vertical one at the sampling point for noise.
Gaussian fuzz is random, distinct bands are deterministic like ISI, and noise on a sloped edge also turns into jitter."
